title: Neural Networks
description: Neurons, layers and activations; the forward pass; what networks can represent; output layers and losses.
overview: A linear model draws a straight boundary. A kernel method draws a curved one by fixing a feature map in advance. A neural network learns the features: it stacks simple units in layers, each layer computing new features from the previous one, so the model itself discovers the representation that makes the task easy.

This chapter defines the network and its forward computation, shows why the nonlinearity between layers is essential, states what networks can and cannot be proved to represent, and fixes the output layers and losses used for regression and classification. The next chapter derives how to train them.
objectives: Write the computation of a single neuron and of a multilayer network in scalar and matrix form.
Compare the common activation functions and explain why a nonlinearity is needed.
Carry out a forward pass by hand and count the parameters of a network.
State the universal approximation theorem and explain why depth helps.
Choose the output layer and loss for regression, binary classification and multiclass classification.

sections.title: The artificial neuron and activation functions
body: A neuron is a tiny decision-maker. It looks at several numbers, decides how much each one matters (the weights), adds them up, and reports how strongly it "fires." For example, a unit that detects "good weather for a picnic" might take temperature and cloud cover as inputs, with a positive weight on temperature, a negative weight on cloud cover and a bias that sets how easily it fires. If the weighted sum is large and positive, the unit outputs a high value. If it is negative, it stays quiet. The nonlinear step at the end is what lets many such units together do more than a single weighted sum could.
An **artificial neuron** (or unit) computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias and passes the result through a nonlinear **activation function** g:
With g the sigmoid this is exactly a logistic regression unit, and with g a hard threshold it is a perceptron. The sum z is the **pre-activation** and a is the activation, or output.

body: The **rectified linear unit** (ReLU) is the default for hidden layers: it is fast and keeps gradients alive in deep networks (see Backpropagation). Sigmoid and softmax appear mostly in output layers.

body.key: Without a nonlinearity, a network is just a linear model. Two linear layers compose into one: W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x. Depth adds power only because of the nonlinearity between the layers.

sections.title: Multilayer networks and the forward pass
body: One neuron can detect one simple pattern. A layer of neurons detects many patterns at once. A second layer then looks at which patterns the first layer found and detects patterns of patterns. In an image network, the first layer might respond to edges, the next to corners and curves built from edges, and the next to shapes such as eyes or wheels. Each layer builds on the previous one. A **multilayer perceptron** (feedforward network) arranges neurons in layers. Every neuron in one layer feeds every neuron in the next, which makes it a **fully connected** layer. Layers between the input and the output are **hidden layers**. Number the layers l = 1, …, L, write a^{[0]} = x for the input, and let n_l be the number of units in layer l. Then
Here W^{[l]} is an n_l × n_{l−1} **weight matrix** and b^{[l]} an n_l-vector of biases. The prediction is the last activation a^{[L]}. Computing it from the input is the **forward pass**.

body.caption: A 3–4–4–2 network. Each line is one weight; each node computes a weighted sum and an activation.

example.title: A forward pass
example.problem: A network has input x = (1, 2), one hidden layer of two ReLU units, and one sigmoid output unit. W^{[1]} = [[0.5, −1], [1, 0.5]], b^{[1]} = (0, 0.5), W^{[2]} = [1, −0.5], b^{[2]} = 0.2. Compute the output.

body: Layer l has n_l(n_{l−1} + 1) parameters. A network with 784 inputs, hidden layers of 128 and 64 units, and 10 outputs has (784·128 + 128) + (128·64 + 64) + (64·10 + 10) = 100,480 + 8,256 + 650 = 109,386 parameters.

To process m examples at once, stack them as the columns of a matrix A^{[0]} ∈ ℝ^{n_0×m}. The same equations hold with Z^{[l]} = W^{[l]}A^{[l−1]} + b^{[l]}1ᵀ, so the forward pass is a sequence of matrix multiplications. This is why networks run well on GPUs.

sections.title: What a hidden layer buys: the XOR example
body: The XOR function (output 1 when exactly one input is 1) cannot be computed by any linear classifier, because the points (0, 1) and (1, 0) cannot be separated from (0, 0) and (1, 1) by a line. This limitation of single-layer perceptrons, pointed out by Minsky and Papert in 1969, stalled the field for a decade. One hidden layer solves it.

example.title: Computing XOR with two ReLU units
example.problem: Let h₁ = ReLU(x₁ + x₂), h₂ = ReLU(x₁ + x₂ − 1), and the output y = h₁ − 2h₂. Verify that y is XOR.
solution: The hidden layer maps the four inputs to new coordinates (h₁, h₂): (0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 0), (2, 1). In this space the two positive cases coincide at (1, 0) and a linear function separates them from the negatives. The hidden layer has learned a feature map that makes the problem linear.

body: This is the central idea of deep learning: the last layer is a linear (or logistic) model on features a^{[L−1]}, and the earlier layers learn those features. Compare a kernel method, where the feature map is chosen by hand, and boosting, where features are added one at a time.

sections.title: Expressive power and the value of depth
body: How large a family of functions do networks cover? The **universal approximation theorem** (Cybenko 1989, Hornik 1991) states that a network with one hidden layer of enough units and a non-polynomial activation can approximate any continuous function on a bounded domain to any desired accuracy.

body.warn: The theorem is an existence result. It does not say how many units are needed (possibly exponentially many), that gradient descent will find the weights, or that the learned function will generalize.

body: A ReLU network computes a **piecewise linear function**. A single hidden layer of N units can create about N linear pieces in one dimension. A deeper network composes functions, and the number of pieces can grow exponentially with the depth. For example, a function such as the sawtooth, which folds the interval repeatedly, needs only a few units per layer but exponentially many units if forced into one hidden layer.

list: **Depth** lets a network reuse intermediate features: edges combine into textures, textures into parts, parts into objects. Many natural functions are compositions of simple pieces, which deep networks represent with far fewer parameters than shallow ones.
**Width** adds capacity at one level of abstraction. Very wide networks behave in some regimes like kernel machines.
In practice, depth is increased with the help of design tricks such as residual connections and normalization (see the next chapters).

body.note: Empirically, networks with far more parameters than training examples can fit random labels, yet still generalize on real data. How they avoid overfitting is a research question (see Generalization on double descent and Learning Theory).

check.q: The universal approximation theorem guarantees that
check.a: a wide enough one-hidden-layer network can approximate any continuous function on a bounded domain
wrong: gradient descent will find the best weights

sections.title: Output layers and losses
body: The output layer and loss follow from the type of target, by the same maximum likelihood logic as the generalized linear models.

Loss
Assumed distribution

body: The raw scores before the output activation are the **logits**. For classification it is numerically safer to compute the loss directly from the logits (the log-sum-exp form of cross-entropy) than to apply softmax and then take a logarithm.

example.title: Loss for the forward-pass example
example.problem: The network in the forward-pass example outputs p = 0.259. Find the binary cross-entropy if the true label is y = 1 and if it is y = 0.
example.solution: For y = 1: −ln 0.259 = 1.35. For y = 0: −ln(1 − 0.259) = −ln 0.741 = 0.30. The network leans toward class 0, so it is penalized heavily when the label is 1.

body: To train, minimize the average loss over the training set, plus any regularization penalty. Because the model is no longer linear in its parameters, this objective is not convex, and gradient-based training only finds a local minimum. In practice, local minima of large networks are usually good enough. The next chapter shows how to compute the gradient efficiently.

quiz.q: A sigmoid unit has weights w = (2, −1), bias b = 0.5, and input x = (1, 3). What is its output?
quiz.why: The pre-activation is 2 − 3 + 0.5 = −0.5, and σ(−0.5) = 1/(1 + e^{0.5}) ≈ 0.38. The value 0.62 is σ(+0.5), and −0.5 is the pre-activation, not the output.

quiz.q: A tanh unit outputs a = 0.6. What is its derivative g′(z) at that point?
quiz.why: For tanh, g′ = 1 − g² = 1 − 0.36 = 0.64. The value 0.24 is g(1 − g), which is the sigmoid derivative formula.

quiz.q: A ReLU unit has a negative pre-activation on every training example. What happens during training?
quiz.a: Its output and gradient are zero on all of them, so its weights stop changing and it is dead
wrong: It outputs negative values and the gradient is −1
It behaves as a linear unit with slope 0.01
It saturates at 1, like a sigmoid unit
quiz.why: ReLU is 0 for z < 0 and its gradient there is 0, so no learning signal reaches the unit's weights. Leaky ReLU was designed to avoid this.

quiz.q: A two-layer network has no activation functions. W₁ is 4 × 3 and W₂ is 2 × 4. The network computes one linear map with a matrix of shape
quiz.why: W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x, and a (2 × 4) times (4 × 3) product is 2 × 3. Without a nonlinearity the two layers collapse into one.

quiz.q: The input is x = (2, 1). The hidden layer has ReLU units with W^{[1]} = [[1, 2], [−1, 1]] and b^{[1]} = (0, 0). The output is the linear unit y = a₁ + 3a₂ − 1. What is y?
How many parameters does a 20–30–10–1 fully connected network have?
quiz.why: Layer l has n_l(n_{l−1} + 1) parameters: 30(21) + 10(31) + 1(11) = 630 + 310 + 11 = 951. Leaving out the biases gives 910.

quiz.q: A layer has 5 units and is fed by a layer of 7 units. A batch of 32 examples is stacked as columns. What is the shape of Z^{[l]}?
quiz.why: Z = WA + b1ᵀ with W of size 5 × 7 and A of size 7 × 32, giving 5 × 32: one column of pre-activations per example.

quiz.q: The XOR network is h₁ = ReLU(x₁ + x₂), h₂ = ReLU(x₁ + x₂ − 1), y = h₁ − 2h₂. What does it output at the input (2, 2)?
quiz.why: h₁ = 4 and h₂ = 3, so y = 4 − 6 = −2. The network computes XOR only on 0/1 inputs, and the output is just a function of the weights elsewhere.

quiz.q: In a deep classification network, how should the final layer be understood in relation to the earlier layers?
quiz.a: As a linear or logistic model applied to features learned by the earlier layers
wrong: As a decision tree applied to the raw inputs
As a layer that selects which earlier layer to trust
As a regularizer that shrinks the earlier weights
quiz.why: The hidden layers learn a feature map, as the XOR example shows, and the output layer then solves a linear problem in that learned space.

quiz.q: A network with a hidden layer of 10,000 units uses the identity activation. What functions can it represent?
quiz.a: Only linear functions of the input
wrong: Any continuous function on a bounded domain
Polynomials of degree up to 10,000
Piecewise linear functions with 10,000 pieces
quiz.why: The universal approximation theorem requires a non-polynomial activation. With the identity, layers compose into a single linear map regardless of width.

quiz.q: A one-hidden-layer ReLU network on a 1-D input makes about N linear pieces with N units. What happens to the number of pieces as ReLU layers are stacked, with a few units per layer?
quiz.a: It can grow exponentially with the depth
wrong: It grows only linearly with the depth
It stays at N, however many layers are added
It grows only with the width of the first layer
quiz.why: Each layer can fold the output of the previous one, so the pieces multiply layer by layer. A single wide layer only adds pieces.

quiz.q: A model predicts the number of insurance claims a customer files in a year, a non-negative integer. Which output layer and loss follow from the chapter's logic?
quiz.a: An exponential output with the Poisson negative log-likelihood
wrong: A sigmoid output with binary cross-entropy
A softmax output with cross-entropy
An identity output with squared error, with no change to the output
quiz.why: Counts are modeled as Poisson, and exp keeps the predicted rate positive. Squared error with an identity output assumes Gaussian noise and can predict negative counts.

quiz.q: A photo may contain any subset of five objects: cat, dog, car, tree, person. Which output layer is appropriate?
quiz.a: Five sigmoid outputs, with a sum of binary cross-entropies
wrong: One softmax over five outputs, with cross-entropy
One sigmoid output, with binary cross-entropy
Five identity outputs, with squared error
quiz.why: Several labels can be true at once, so each is an independent Bernoulli. Softmax forces the probabilities to sum to 1, which allows only one label.

quiz.q: A 3-class softmax receives the logits (0, 0, 0). The true class is the second. What is the cross-entropy loss?
quiz.why: Equal logits give p = 1/3 for each class, so the loss is −ln(1/3) = ln 3 ≈ 1.10. The value 0.48 is log₁₀ 3, a different base.

quiz.q: A sigmoid output gives p = 0.8, and the true label is y = 0. What is the binary cross-entropy?
quiz.why: For y = 0 the loss is −ln(1 − p) = −ln 0.2 = 1.61. The value 0.22 is −ln 0.8, the loss if the label were 1.

quiz.q: Which statement about the training objective of a neural network is correct?
quiz.a: It is not convex in the parameters, so different initializations can reach different solutions
wrong: It is convex whenever the loss is cross-entropy, so a global minimum is guaranteed
It becomes convex once the network is wide enough
It is not convex, so gradient descent cannot reduce the loss
quiz.why: The hidden layers make the output depend nonlinearly on the weights, so the objective is non-convex. Gradient descent still lowers the loss and finds a local minimum, usually good enough.

quiz.q: Why is it better to compute a classification loss directly from the logits than to apply softmax and then take a logarithm?
quiz.a: The log-sum-exp form avoids overflow and underflow in the exponentials
wrong: Softmax is not differentiable for large logits
The two methods give different loss values, and the direct one is correct
Softmax probabilities do not sum to 1 in floating point
quiz.why: Exponentials of large logits overflow and tiny probabilities underflow to 0, making the log undefined. The two forms are mathematically equal, but the direct one is stable.

summary: A neuron computes g(wᵀx + b). A layer applies this to every unit, and a network chains layers: z^{[l]} = W^{[l]}a^{[l−1]} + b^{[l]}, a^{[l]} = g(z^{[l]}).
The nonlinearity is essential: without it the network is linear. ReLU is the standard hidden activation; sigmoid and softmax are used at the output.
A hidden layer learns features that make the task linearly solvable, as in the XOR example. Parameter counts are n_l(n_{l−1} + 1) per layer.
One-hidden-layer networks are universal approximators, but the theorem says nothing about size or learnability. Depth gives efficient compositional representations.

Choose the output and loss by the target: identity and squared error for regression, sigmoid and cross-entropy for binary labels, softmax and cross-entropy for classes. The training objective is non-convex.

problems.q: Compute the forward pass for x = (1, −1), W^{[1]} = [[1, 1], [−1, 2]], b^{[1]} = (0, 1), ReLU hidden units, and output z = 2a₁ + a₂ − 1 with a linear output unit.
A network has layer sizes 10–50–50–3. Count its parameters.
Show that the XOR network h₁ = ReLU(x₁ + x₂), h₂ = ReLU(x₁ + x₂ − 1), y = h₁ − 2h₂ gives y = 0 at (1, 1) and y = 1 at (0, 1).
A softmax output has logits (2, 0, −1) and the true class is the first. Find the probabilities and the cross-entropy loss.
Why can a deep ReLU network represent a function with exponentially many linear pieces using only a polynomial number of units?
problems.solution: Each layer can apply a fold to the output of the previous one (for example the map x → 2 min(x, 1 − x) on [0, 1], which takes two ReLU units). Composing k such layers gives a sawtooth with 2^k pieces using about 2k units. A single hidden layer would need about 2^k units to create 2^k pieces.
problems.a: Composition multiplies the number of pieces layer by layer, while width only adds pieces.
